subtopics.title: Particle nature of matter

slots.X: Explain why a tiny coloured drop can eventually tint the entire closed beaker without adding more dye.
slots.Y: A drop of dye spreads through still water. What unseen moving entities can explain this change? Link invisible random molecular motion to visible changes in concentration; distinguish observation from inference.
slots.Z: A clear region becomes slightly coloured as dye particles cross into it and redistribute while total particle number stays fixed.
slots.W: Learner independently performs the decisive EXPLAIN inference required by: Explain why a tiny coloured drop can eventually tint the entire closed beaker without adding more dye.

qrt_instances.student_task: Explain why a tiny coloured drop can eventually tint the entire closed beaker without adding more dye.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: The coloured substance multiplies as it spreads.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Track a fixed set of dye particles through successive snapshots.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Draw a beaker before and after mixing using distinguishable particle dots. Keep the same particle count in the closed-beaker diagram; vary positions rather than transforming water molecules into new species.
qrt_instances.independent_check: Check conservation for a declared system boundary.

slots.X: A red solute disperses without gas, heat or precipitate. What simple model best explains the uniform red appearance, and what would further test it?
slots.Y: A drop of dye spreads through still water. What unseen moving entities can explain this change? An observation of uniform colour does not establish formation of a new chemical substance. A model must predict a distinguishing observation.
slots.Z: Simple diffusion changes position and concentration; reaction changes species identities. A colour change could have either cause in other experiments.

subtopics.title: States, particle motion and compressibility

slots.X: A sealed air syringe compresses easily, but the same syringe filled with water barely compresses. Explain.
slots.Y: Why is it difficult to squeeze liquid water into half its original volume but easy to compress air? Connect particle spacing with bulk compressibility, while accounting for a sealed container and constant particle identities.
slots.Z: Halve the syringe volume without losing air. Same particles, smaller typical distances; pressure generally rises.
slots.W: Learner independently performs the decisive EXPLAIN inference required by: A sealed air syringe compresses easily, but the same syringe filled with water barely compresses. Explain.

qrt_instances.student_task: A sealed air syringe compresses easily, but the same syringe filled with water barely compresses. Explain.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Gases compress because their molecules shrink.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Draw the same-sized particles in a smaller box with reduced gaps.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Three equal-size boxes depict closely packed ordered solid particles, disordered close-packed liquid particles and widely separated gas particles. A fourth box compresses a gas while keeping particle number fixed.
qrt_instances.independent_check: Identify the system boundary and whether the particle number is fixed.

slots.Y: Why is it difficult to squeeze liquid water into half its original volume but easy to compress air? A model should distinguish mobility, fixed relative positions and compressibility rather than use 'particles far apart' for every state.
slots.Z: The gas model predicts large volume response to pressure; the liquid model predicts flow but small ordinary compressibility.

subtopics.title: Diffusion and mixing

slots.X: How can a net diffusion flux occur when no molecule 'knows' which way to move?
slots.Y: Why does the smell of food move through a room even when no fan is running? Random motion occurs in both directions, yet more particles leave a dense region than enter it because the count is higher there.
slots.Z: Take two equal adjacent volumes with 100 and 5 fragrance particles. Random crossing from the dense region gives more net outward crossings until concentrations approach.
slots.W: Learner independently performs the decisive EXPLAIN inference required by: How can a net diffusion flux occur when no molecule 'knows' which way to move?

qrt_instances.student_task: How can a net diffusion flux occur when no molecule 'knows' which way to move?
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Each perfume molecule travels directly from the source toward the observer.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Distinguish random particle trajectories from the evolving concentration profile.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Use random arrows to show molecules moving in all directions and shading for the concentration gradient. A separate large air-flow arrow represents bulk convection; do not confuse the two.
qrt_instances.independent_check: At equilibrium net flux approaches zero; motion persists.

slots.Z: Repeat a perfume test with controlled air currents to distinguish bulk transport from molecular diffusion.

subtopics.title: Evaporation and cooling

slots.X: Explain why wet clothes can feel cold in moving air even when the air is warm.
slots.Y: Why can evaporation cool the remaining liquid even on a warm day? Connect a molecular energy distribution, surface escape and cooling of the remaining sample.
slots.Z: Fast-escaping molecules remove more-than-average energy from the liquid and the environment may supply replacement heat.
slots.W: Learner independently performs the decisive EXPLAIN inference required by: Explain why wet clothes can feel cold in moving air even when the air is warm.

qrt_instances.student_task: Explain why wet clothes can feel cold in moving air even when the air is warm.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: Evaporation only occurs at the boiling point.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Distinguish surface evaporation from bulk boiling.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Draw liquid molecules with a spread of motion-arrow lengths. Show some high-energy surface molecules escaping; the remaining ones have lower average energy unless heat enters.
qrt_instances.independent_check: Check an energy pathway, not just the sensation.

slots.Z: A wide shallow dish often loses water faster than a narrow deep glass at similar temperatures because its exposed area is larger.

subtopics.title: Heating curves and latent heat (scope check)

slots.X: Explain why a melting sample can remain near 0°C while energy continues entering.
slots.Y: Why can an ice-water mixture continue absorbing heat while the thermometer stays near the melting temperature? Energy conservation connects heater input to phase change while temperature is approximately fixed.
slots.Z: For ice at its melting temperature, supplied heat changes solid to liquid rather than warming the liquid until melting is complete.
slots.W: Learner independently performs the decisive EXPLAIN inference required by: Explain why a melting sample can remain near 0°C while energy continues entering.

qrt_instances.student_task: Explain why a melting sample can remain near 0°C while energy continues entering.
qrt_instances.wrong_idea: A horizontal heating curve means no energy enters the material.
qrt_instances.replacement_rule: Track heat input and microscopic changes separately.
qrt_instances.visual_job: Sketch a temperature-versus-energy plot: sloping solid heating, flat melting, sloping liquid heating. Label the plateau as energy used for phase change, not 'heater turned off'.
qrt_instances.independent_check: Point to the phase fraction and heat-input assumptions.
